title: Sudoku Solver
spaceBreakdown:
- int rows[9], cols[9], boxes[9]: 27 fixed-size ints → O(1)
- recursion call-stack: depth up to k (number of empty cells, ≤ 81) → O(k)
- not counted: input board (modified in place)
approach: Use backtracking with bitmask constraint tracking. Maintain three arrays of 9-bit masks (one per row, column, and 3×3 box) recording which digits are already placed. At each step, select the empty cell with the fewest legal candidates (Minimum Remaining Values heuristic) to minimize branching. Try each candidate, recurse, and undo on failure. The MRV heuristic, combined with early termination when a cell has zero candidates, prunes the search tree aggressively enough that any valid 9×9 Sudoku is solved near-instantly.
hints: When you write a digit into an empty cell, how does that change the set of digits that are still legal for every other empty cell sharing its row, column, or 3×3 box? The board is always 9×9 with a guaranteed unique solution.

Backtracking with bitmask constraint tracking. Maintain three 9-bit masks per row/col/box of used digits; always expand the empty cell with the fewest candidates (MRV heuristic). In Example 1, cell (0,2) has candidates {1,2,4} since row 0 uses {3,5,7}, column 2 uses {8}, and box 0 uses {3,5,6,8,9}.

```
function solve(filled):
    if filled == 81: return true
    scan all empty cells, find one with fewest candidates (MRV)
    if any empty cell has 0 candidates: return false
    for each candidate digit d in that cell:
        place d in board, set bit in row/col/box masks
        if solve(filled + 1): return true
        clear bit in row/col/box masks, restore cell to '.'
    return false
```

followUps.q: Generalize to an N×N Sudoku where N is a perfect square (e.g., 16×16 with hex digits).
followUps.a: Replace the 9-bit masks with N-bit masks and change the box index formula to (r / √N) * √N + (c / √N). The MRV heuristic and backtracking structure remain identical. TC becomes O(N^k) where k is the number of empty cells; SC becomes O(N + k) for the masks and recursion stack.

followUps.q: Determine whether a given puzzle has a unique solution.
followUps.a: After finding the first solution, continue the backtracking search for a second one instead of returning immediately. If a second solution is found, the puzzle is not unique. TC is at most twice the solving time in the worst case (two full solutions explored), SC unchanged.

followUps.q: Solve the puzzle using Algorithm X with Dancing Links instead of bitmask backtracking.
followUps.a: Model Sudoku as an exact cover problem: each row of the matrix represents placing a specific digit in a specific cell, with columns for cell-constraints, row-constraints, column-constraints, and box-constraints. Dancing Links efficiently removes and restores rows during backtracking. TC is still exponential in the worst case but typically faster for sparse puzzles; SC is O(N²) for the link structure versus O(N) for bitmasks.
